danish.title: Ellevte bog (1812) — Kapitel 33
paragraphs: Den tredje september vågnede Pierre sent. Han havde hovedpine, tøjet, som han havde sovet i uden at klæde sig af, føltes ubehageligt på kroppen, og hans sind bar et svagt minde om noget skamfuldt, han havde gjort dagen før. Det skamfulde var hans samtale med kaptajn Ramballe dagen før.

Klokken var elleve, men det syntes usædvanligt mørkt udenfor. Pierre rejste sig, gned øjnene og fik øje på pistolen med det graverede skæfte, som Gerásim havde lagt tilbage på skrivebordet, og huskede, hvor han var, og hvad der ventede ham netop den dag.
»Er jeg for sent på den?« tænkte han. »Nej, han gør nok ikke sit indtog i Moskva før middag.«
Pierre tillod sig ikke at tænke over, hvad der lå foran ham, men skyndte sig at handle.

Efter at have ordnet sit tøj tog han pistolen og ville til at gå ud. Men da faldt det ham for første gang ind, at han bestemt ikke kunne bære våbenet i hånden gennem gaderne. Det var vanskeligt at skjule en så stor pistol selv under hans vide frakke. Han kunne ikke bære den ubemærket i bæltet eller under armen. Desuden var den affyret, og han havde ikke haft tid til at lade den igen. »Lige meget, dolken klarer det,« sagde han til sig selv, skønt han under planlægningen af sit forehavende mere end én gang var nået til den konklusion, at den afgørende fejl, studenten i 1809 begik, var at forsøge at dræbe Napoleon med en dolk. Men da hans hovedformål ikke bestod i at gennemføre sin plan, men i at bevise over for sig selv, at han ikke ville opgive sin beslutning og gjorde alt, hvad han kunne, for at nå sit mål, tog Pierre hastigt den stumpe, takkede dolk i en grøn skede, som han havde købt på Sukharev-markedet sammen med pistolen, og gemte den under sin vest.
Efter at have bundet et bælte over frakken og trukket sin kasket dybt ned i panden gik Pierre ned ad gangen, idet han forsøgte at undgå at støje eller møde kaptajnen, og passerede ud på gaden.

Ildebranden, som han havde betragtet med så megen ligegyldighed aftenen før, var tiltaget voldsomt i løbet af natten. Moskva brændte flere steder. Bygningerne i Vognrækken på den anden side af floden, i Bazaren og ved Povarskój samt pramme på Moskva-floden og tømmerpladserne ved Dorogomílov-broen stod alle i lys lue.

Pierres vej førte gennem sidegader til Povarskój og derfra til Sankt Nikolaj-kirken ved Arbat, hvor han for længe siden havde besluttet, at handlingen skulle finde sted. Portene til de fleste huse var låst og skodderne slået for. Gaderne og stræder lå øde. Luften var fuld af røg og lugten af brand. Nu og da mødte han russere med ængstelige og sky ansigter, og franskmænd med et udseende ikke som byboere men som soldater i felten, der gik midt på gaden. Både russerne og franskmændene stirrede forundret på Pierre. Ud over hans højde og fyldighed og det underlige dystre udtryk af lidelse i hans ansigt og hele skikkelse gloede russerne på Pierre, fordi de ikke kunne afgøre, hvilken stand han tilhørte. Franskmændene fulgte ham med forbavsede blikke, hovedsageligt fordi Pierre, i modsætning til alle de andre russere, der så på franskmændene med frygt og nysgerrighed, ikke skænkede dem nogen opmærksomhed. Ved porten til et hus standsede tre franskmænd, der forklarede noget til nogle russere, som ikke forstod dem, Pierre og spurgte, om han ikke talte fransk.

Pierre rystede på hovedet og gik videre. I en anden sidegade råbte en skildvagt, der stod ved en grøn ammunitionsvogn, af ham, men først da råbet truende blev gentaget, og han hørte klikket af mandens musket, da han løftede den, forstod Pierre, at han skulle gå over på den anden side af gaden. Han hørte intet og så intet af, hvad der foregik omkring ham. Han bar sin beslutning i sig med rædsel og hast, som noget forfærdeligt og fremmed, for efter den foregående nats oplevelse var han bange for at miste den. Men han var ikke bestemt til at nå sit mål med sindsroen i behold. Og selv om intet havde hindret ham undervejs, kunne hans forsæt ikke længere være blevet ført ud i livet, for Napoleon havde passeret Arbat mere end fire timer forinden på sin vej fra Dorogomílov-forstaden til Kreml og sad nu i et meget dystert humør i et kejserligt kabinet i Kreml og udstedte detaljerede og præcise ordrer om foranstaltninger, der straks skulle træffes for at slukke branden, forhindre plyndring og berolige indbyggerne. Men det vidste Pierre ikke; han var helt opslugt af det, der lå foran ham, og blev pint — som alle, der stædigt påtager sig en opgave, der er umulig for dem, ikke på grund af dens vanskelighed men på grund af dens uforenelighed med deres natur — af frygten for at vakle i det afgørende øjeblik og derved miste sin selvrespekt.
Skønt han hverken hørte eller så noget omkring sig, fandt han ad instinktets vej og tog ikke fejl i de sidegader, der førte til Povarskój.

Da Pierre nærmede sig den gade, blev røgen tættere og tættere — han kunne endog mærke varmen fra ilden. Hist og her slog krøllede flammetunger op under husternes tage. Han mødte flere mennesker på gaden, og de var mere ophidsede. Men Pierre, skønt han fornemmede, at der foregik noget usædvanligt omkring ham, indså ikke, at han nærmede sig branden. Mens han gik ad en gangsti over et stort åbent areal, der på den ene side grænsede op til Povarskój og på den anden til fyrst Gruzínskijs haves, hørte Pierre pludselig en kvindes fortvivlede gråd tæt ved. Han standsede, som om han vågnede af en drøm, og løftede hovedet.

Ved siden af stien, på det støvede tørre græs, lå alle slags husholdningsgenstande i en bunke: dyner, en samovar, ikoner og kufferter. På jorden ved siden af kufferterne sad en mager kvinde, ikke helt ung, med lange fremstående fortænder og iført en sort kappe og hue. Denne kvinde, der vuggende frem og tilbage mumlede noget, kvaltes af hulk. To piger på omkring ti og tolv år, klædt i beskidte korte kjoler og kapper, stirrede på deres mor med et udtryk af lamslåethed i de blege, forskræmte ansigter. Det mindste barn, en dreng på omkring syv, der bar en overfrakke og en kæmpemæssig kasket, der tydeligvis ikke var hans egen, græd i sin gamle barnepiges arme. En beskidt, barfodet stuepige sad på en kuffert og havde løst sin lyse fletning og trak i den, mens hun snøftede over sit svedne hår. Kvindens mand, en lille rundskuldret mand i den civile embedsmands hverdagsuniform, med pølseformede bakkenbarter, og med håret glatkæmmet frem over tindingerne synligt under den firkantede kasket, flyttede med udtryksløst ansigt de kufferter, der stod oven på hinanden, og trak noget tøj frem under dem.
Så snart hun fik øje på Pierre, kastede kvinden sig næsten for hans fødder.

»Kære mennesker, gode kristne, red mig, hjælp mig, kære venner... hjælp os, nogen,« mumlede hun mellem sine hulk. »Min pige... Min datter! Min yngste datter er efterladt. Hun er brændt! Åh! Var det for dette, jeg ammede dig.... Åh!«

»Lad være, Marja Nikolajevna!« sagde hendes mand til hende med lav stemme, åbenbart kun for at retfærdiggøre sig over for den fremmede. »Søster har sikkert taget hende med, ellers hvor kan hun være?« tilføjede han.

»Uhyre! Skurk!« råbte kvinden vredt, idet hun pludselig holdt op med at græde. »Du har intet hjerte, du føler ikke for dit eget barn! En anden mand ville have reddet hende fra ilden. Men dette er et uhyre og hverken en mand eller en far! De, ærede herre, er en ædel mand,« fortsatte hun og henvendte sig hurtigt til Pierre mellem sine hulk. »Ilden brød ud ved siden af os og blæste hen mod os, pigen råbte 'Ildebrand!' og vi styrtede ud for at samle vores ting. Vi løb ud, som vi var.... Det her er, hvad vi fik med.... Ikonerne og min medgiftsseng, alt det andet er tabt. Vi greb børnene. Men ikke Katja! Åh! Åh, Herre!...« og igen begyndte hun at hulke. »Mit barn, min kære! Brændt, brændt!«
»Men hvor blev hun efterladt?« spurgte Pierre.
Af udtrykket i hans livfulde ansigt kunne kvinden se, at denne mand måske kunne hjælpe hende.

»Åh, kære herre!« råbte hun og greb ham om benene. »Min velgører, berolig mit hjerte.... Aníska, gå, din fæle pige, vis ham vejen!« råbte hun til stuepigen, idet hun vredt åbnede munden og blottede sine lange tænder endnu mere.
»Vis mig vejen, vis mig, jeg... jeg klarer det,« stammede Pierre hastigt.

Den beskidte stuepige trådte frem bag kufferten, ordnede sin fletning, sukkede og gik af sted på sine korte bare fødder ad stien. Pierre følte, som om han var vendt tilbage til livet efter en dyb afmagt. Han holdt hovedet højere, hans øjne lyste af livskraft, og med hurtige skridt fulgte han stuepigen, indhentede hende og nåede ud til Povarskój. Hele gaden var fuld af skyer af sort røg. Flammetunger brød hist og her igennem skyen. En stor mængde mennesker stod foran ilden. Midt på gaden stod en fransk general og sagde noget til dem omkring sig. Pierre, ledsaget af stuepigen, var på vej hen mod det sted, hvor generalen stod, men de franske soldater standsede ham.
»On ne passe pas!« råbte en stemme.
»Her kommer I ikke igennem!«
»Herhen, onkel,« råbte pigen. »Vi går gennem sidegaden, forbi Nikúlinernes!«
Pierre vendte om og sprang nu og da for at følge med hende. Hun løb over gaden, drejede ned ad en sidegade til venstre og drejede efter tre huse ind i en gård til højre.

»Det er herinde, lige i nærheden,« sagde hun og løb over gården, åbnede en låge i et træplankeværk og pegede hen på en lille træfløj af huset, der brændte klart og voldsomt. Den ene side var styrtet sammen, den anden stod i brand, og klare flammer slog ud af vinduesåbningerne og under taget.
Da Pierre passerede gennem lågen, blev han indhyllet i hed luft og standsede ufrivilligt.
»Hvilket hus? Hvilket er jeres hus?« spurgte han.

»Åh!« jamrede pigen og pegede på fløjbygningen. »Det dér, det var vores bolig. Du er brændt til døde, vores skat, Katja, min dyrebare lille frøken! Åh!« klagede Aníska, som ved synet af branden følte, at hun også måtte give udtryk for sine følelser.

Pierre styrtede hen mod fløjen, men heden var så voldsom, at han ufrivilligt slog en bue udenom og nåede hen til det store hus, der endnu kun brændte i den ene ende lige under taget, og hvortil en flok franskmænd havde samlet sig. Først forstod Pierre ikke, hvad disse mænd, der slæbte noget ud, foretog sig; men da han foran sig så en franskmand, der slog en bonde med en stump sabel og forsøgte at tage en ræveskindskappe fra ham, forstod han vagt, at der foregik plyndring, men han havde ikke tid til at dvæle ved den tanke.

Lyden af knitren og larm fra sammenstyrtende vægge og lofter, fløjten og hvæsen fra flammerne, de ophidsede råb fra menneskene og synet af den bølgende røg, der snart samlede sig i tykke sorte skyer og snart steg til vejrs med glittrende gnister, med tætte flammeknipper her og der (snart røde og snart som gyldne fiskeskæl, der krøb langs væggene), samt heden og røgen og bevægelsernes hastighed virkede på Pierre med den sædvanlige oplivende virkning, en brand har. Den havde en særligt stærk virkning på ham, fordi han ved synet af ilden pludselig følte sig befriet fra de tanker, der havde tynget ham. Han følte sig ung, klar, smidig og beslutsom. Han løb rundt om til den anden side af fløjen og var ved at styrte ind i den del, der endnu stod, da han lige over sit hoved hørte flere stemmer råbe og derpå en knagende lyd og drønet af noget tungt, der faldt ned tæt ved ham.

Pierre kiggede op og så i et vindue i det store hus nogle franskmænd, der netop havde kastet en kommodeskuffe fyldt med metalgenstande ud. Andre franske soldater, der stod nedenfor, gik hen til skuffen.
»Hvad vil den fyr?« råbte en af dem og hentydede til Pierre.
»Der er et barn i det hus. Har I ikke set et barn?« råbte Pierre.

»Hvad snakker han om? Forsvind herfra!« sagde flere stemmer, og en af soldaterne, der åbenbart var bange for, at Pierre ville tage noget af det sølvtøj og bronze, der var i skuffen, bevægede sig truende mod ham.
»Et barn?« råbte en franskmand ovenfra. »Jeg hørte godt nok noget pippe inde i haven. Måske er det hans unge, han leder efter. Man skal jo trods alt være menneskelig, ikke sandt...«
»Hvor? Hvor?« sagde Pierre.
»Derhenne! Derhenne!« råbte franskmanden i vinduet og pegede mod haven bag huset. »Vent lidt — jeg kommer ned.«
Og et minut eller to senere sprang franskmanden, en sortøjet fyr med en plet på kinden, i skjorteærmer, virkelig ud af et vindue i stueetagen, klappede Pierre på skulderen og løb med ham ind i haven.
»Skynd jer, I andre!« råbte han til sine kammerater. »Det bliver hedt herinde.«
Da de nåede en grussti bag huset, trak franskmanden Pierre i armen og pegede på et rundt, gruset areal, hvor en treårig pige i en lyserød kjole lå under en bænk.

»Dér er dit barn! Åh, en pige, desto bedre!« sagde franskmanden. »Farvel, Tyksakken. Vi er nødt til at være menneskelige, vi er alle dødelige, ved du nok!« og franskmanden med pletten på kinden løb tilbage til sine kammerater.

Forpustet af glæde løb Pierre hen til den lille pige og ville tage hende i sine arme. Men da hun så en fremmed, begyndte det sygelige, skrofuløse barn, der lignede sin mor på en uheldig måde, at skrige og løbe væk. Pierre greb hende dog og løftede hende op i sine arme. Hun skreg fortvivlet og vredt og forsøgte med sine små hænder at rive Pierres hænder bort og bide i dem med sin savlende mund. Pierre blev grebet af en følelse af rædsel og afsky, som den han havde oplevet ved at røre et væmmeligt lille dyr. Men han anstrengte sig for ikke at kaste barnet fra sig og løb med hende hen til det store hus. Det var nu imidlertid umuligt at komme tilbage den vej, han var kommet; stuepigen Aníska var der ikke længere, og Pierre trykkede med en følelse af medlidenhed og afsky det våde, smertefuldt grædende barn til sig så ømt, han kunne, og løb med hende gennem haven for at finde en anden udvej.

english.title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 33
paragraphs: On the third of September Pierre woke late. His head ached, the clothes in which he had slept without undressing felt uncomfortable on his body, and his mind held a dim awareness of something shameful he had done the day before. That something shameful was his conversation with Captain Ramballe.

It was eleven by the clock, but it seemed peculiarly dark outside. Pierre got up, rubbed his eyes, and seeing the engraved pistol which Gerasim had replaced on the writing table, remembered where he was and what lay before him that day.
"Am I too late?" he thought. "No, probably he won't enter Moscow before noon."
Pierre did not allow himself to think about what lay ahead, but hurried to act.

After adjusting his clothes, he took the pistol and was about to go out. But then it occurred to him for the first time that he certainly could not carry the weapon in his hand through the streets. It was hard to hide such a big pistol even under his wide coat. He could not carry it unnoticed in his belt or under his arm. Besides, it had been fired and he had not had time to reload it. "No matter, the dagger will do," he said to himself, though when planning his design he had more than once concluded that the chief mistake of the student who tried to kill Napoleon in 1809 was trying to do it with a dagger. But since his chief purpose was not really to carry out his plan, but to prove to himself that he would not abandon his intention and was doing everything he could to achieve it, Pierre hastily took the blunt, jagged dagger in a green sheath which he had bought with the pistol at the Sukharev market and hid it under his waistcoat.
Tying a belt over his coat and pulling his cap low on his head, Pierre went down the corridor, trying to avoid making noise or meeting the captain, and slipped out into the street.

The fire, which he had looked at so indifferently the evening before, had grown enormously during the night. Moscow was burning in several places. The buildings in Carriage Row, across the river, in the Bazaar and the Povarskoy, as well as the barges on the Moscow River and the timber yards by the Dorogomilov Bridge, were all ablaze.

Pierre's way led through side streets to the Povarskoy and from there to the church of St. Nicholas on the Arbat, where he had long before decided the deed should be done. The gates of most houses were locked and the shutters up. The streets and lanes were deserted. The air was full of smoke and the smell of burning. Now and then he met Russians with anxious, timid faces, and Frenchmen with a look not of the city but of the camp, walking in the middle of the streets. Both the Russians and the French looked at Pierre with surprise. Besides his height and stoutness, and the strange, gloomy look of suffering in his face and whole figure, the Russians stared at Pierre because they could not figure out what class he belonged to. The French followed him with astonishment mainly because Pierre, unlike all the other Russians who gazed at them with fear and curiosity, paid no attention to them. At the gate of one house, three Frenchmen who were trying to explain something to some Russians who did not understand them stopped Pierre and asked if he spoke French.

Pierre shook his head and went on. In another side street a sentinel beside a green ammunition wagon shouted at him, but only when the shout was repeated threateningly and he heard the click of the man's musket did Pierre understand that he had to cross to the other side of the street. He heard nothing and saw nothing of what went on around him. He carried his resolution within himself with terror and haste, like something dreadful and alien, for after the previous night's experience he was afraid of losing it. But he was not destined to bring his mood safely to its destination. And even had nothing hindered him along the way, his intention could not now have been carried out, for Napoleon had passed the Arbat more than four hours earlier on his way from the Dorogomilov suburb to the Kremlin, and was now sitting in a very gloomy mood in a royal study in the Kremlin, giving detailed orders for measures to extinguish the fire, prevent looting, and reassure the inhabitants. But Pierre did not know this; entirely absorbed in what lay before him, he was tortured—as are all those who stubbornly undertake a task impossible for them not because of its difficulty but because of its incompatibility with their nature—by the fear of weakening at the decisive moment and losing his self-respect.
Though he heard and saw nothing around him, he found his way by instinct and did not go wrong in the side streets leading to the Povarskoy.

As Pierre approached that street, the smoke became denser and denser—he could even feel the heat of the fire. Occasionally tongues of flame curled out from under the roofs of buildings. He met more people in the streets, and they were more agitated. But Pierre, though he sensed that something unusual was happening around him, did not realize he was approaching the fire. As he walked along a footpath across a wide-open space adjoining the Povarskoy on one side and the gardens of Prince Gruzinsky's house on the other, Pierre suddenly heard a woman's desperate weeping close to him. He stopped as if awakening from a dream and lifted his head.

By the side of the path, on the dusty dry grass, all sorts of household goods lay in a heap: featherbeds, a samovar, icons, and trunks. On the ground, beside the trunks, sat a thin woman no longer young, with long, prominent upper teeth, wearing a black cloak and cap. This woman, swaying back and forth and muttering something, was choking with sobs. Two girls of about ten and twelve, dressed in dirty short frocks and cloaks, were staring at their mother with stupefied, pale, frightened faces. The youngest child, a boy of about seven wearing an overcoat and an enormous cap that was obviously not his own, was crying in his old nurse's arms. A dirty, barefooted maid was sitting on a trunk, having undone her pale-colored braid, and was pulling it straight and sniffing at her singed hair. The woman's husband, a short, round-shouldered man in the undress uniform of a civilian official, with sausage-shaped whiskers and hair smoothly brushed forward over his temples under his square-set cap, was moving the trunks, which were placed one on another, and dragging some garments from under them, his face expressionless.
As soon as she saw Pierre, the woman almost threw herself at his feet.

"Dear people, good Christians, save me, help me, dear friends... help us, somebody," she sobbed. "My girl... My daughter! My youngest daughter was left behind. She's burned! Oh! Was it for this I nursed you... Oh!"
"Don't, Maria Nikolaevna!" said her husband to her in a low voice, evidently only to justify himself before the stranger. "Sister must have taken her, or else where can she be?" he added.

"Monster! Villain!" shouted the woman angrily, suddenly ceasing to weep. "You have no heart, you don't care about your own child! Another man would have rescued her from the fire. But this is a monster, not a man, not a father! You, honored sir, are a noble man," she went on, addressing Pierre rapidly between her sobs. "The fire broke out next door, and blew our way, the maid called out 'Fire!' and we rushed to grab our things. We ran out just as we were... This is what we saved... The icons, and my dowry bed, everything else is lost. We grabbed the children. But not Katie! Oh, Lord!..." and again she began to sob. "My child, my darling! Burned, burned!"
"But where was she left?" asked Pierre.
From the expression on his engaged face, the woman saw that this man might help her.

"Oh, dear sir!" she cried, seizing him by the legs. "My savior, give me some peace of mind... Aniska, go, you horrible girl, show him the way!" she cried to the maid, angrily opening her mouth and further exposing her long teeth.
"Show me the way, show me, I... I'll do it," gasped Pierre rapidly.

The dirty maid stepped from behind the trunk, put up her braid, sighed, and went on her short, bare feet along the path. Pierre felt as if he had come back to life after a heavy swoon. He held his head higher, his eyes shone with the light of life, and with swift steps he followed the maid, overtook her, and came out on the Povarskoy. The whole street was full of clouds of black smoke. Tongues of flame here and there broke through the clouds. A great number of people crowded in front of the fire. In the middle of the street stood a French general saying something to those around him. Pierre, accompanied by the maid, was heading toward the spot where the general stood, but the French soldiers stopped him.
"You can't pass!" cried a voice.
* "You can't pass!"
"This way, uncle," cried the girl. "We'll get through the side street, by the Nikulins'!"
Pierre turned back, breaking into a run now and then to keep up with her. She ran across the street, turned down a side street to the left, and passing three houses, turned into a yard on the right.

"It's here, right nearby," said she, and running across the yard, opened a gate in a wooden fence and, stopping, pointed out to him a small wooden wing of the house that was burning brightly and fiercely. One side had fallen in, another was on fire, and bright flames poured from the openings of the windows and from under the roof.
As Pierre passed through the fence gate, he was enveloped by hot air and involuntarily stopped.
"Which is it? Which is your house?" he asked.

"Ooh!" wailed the girl, pointing to the wing. "That's it, that was our home. You've burned to death, our darling, Katie, my precious little girl! Ooh!" lamented Aniska, who at the sight of the fire felt she too must express her feelings.

Pierre rushed to the wing, but the heat was so great that he involuntarily swerved in a curve and came upon the large house that was as yet burning only at one end, just below the roof, and around which swarmed a crowd of Frenchmen. At first Pierre did not realize what these men were doing, dragging things out; but seeing a Frenchman hitting a peasant with a flat saber, trying to take a fox-fur coat from him, he vaguely understood that looting was going on, though he had no time to dwell on the thought.

The sounds of crackling and the crash of falling walls and ceilings, the whistle and hiss of the flames, the excited shouts of the people, and the sight of the swaying smoke—now gathering into thick black clouds, now rising with glittering sparks, with here and there dense sheaves of flame (now red and now like golden fish scales creeping along the walls)—and the heat and smoke and speed of movement all produced on Pierre the usual stimulating effects of a fire. It had a particularly strong effect on him because at the sight of the fire he felt himself suddenly freed from the ideas that had weighed him down. He felt young, bright, nimble, and resolute. He ran around to the other side of the wing and was about to dash into the part still standing when just above his head he heard several voices shouting, then a cracking sound and the ring of something heavy falling close beside him.

Pierre looked up and saw at a window of the large house some Frenchmen who had just thrown out the drawer of a chest, filled with metal articles. Other French soldiers standing below went up to the drawer.
"What does this fellow want?" shouted one of them, referring to Pierre.
"There's a child in that house. Haven't you seen a child?" cried Pierre.

"What's he talking about? Get along!" said several voices, and one of the soldiers, evidently afraid Pierre might try to take some of the plate and bronzes in the drawer, moved threateningly toward him.
"A child?" shouted a Frenchman from above. "I did hear something squealing in the garden. Maybe it's his kid the fellow is looking for. After all, one must be humane, you know..."
"Where is it? Where?" said Pierre.
"There! There!" shouted the Frenchman at the window, pointing to the garden at the back of the house. "Wait a bit—I'm coming down."

And a minute or two later the Frenchman, a dark-eyed fellow with a spot on his cheek, in shirtsleeves, really did jump out of a ground-floor window and, clapping Pierre on the shoulder, ran with him into the garden.
"Hurry up, you others!" he called to his comrades. "It's getting hot."
When they reached a gravel path behind the house, the Frenchman pulled Pierre by the arm and pointed to a round, graveled space where a three-year-old girl in a pink dress was lying under a bench.

"There's your child! Oh, a girl, so much the better!" said the Frenchman. "Goodbye, Fatty. We must be humane—we're all mortal, you know!" and the Frenchman with the spot on his cheek ran back to his comrades.

Breathless with joy, Pierre ran to the little girl and was about to pick her up. But seeing a stranger, the sickly, scrofulous-looking child—unattractively like her mother—began to scream and run away. Pierre, however, seized her and lifted her in his arms. She screamed desperately and angrily, trying with her little hands to pull Pierre's hands away and to bite them with her slobbering mouth. Pierre was seized by a feeling of horror and revulsion, like touching some nasty little animal. But he made an effort not to drop the child and ran with her toward the large house. It was now impossible to get back the way he had come; the maid, Aniska, was no longer there, and Pierre, with a feeling of pity and disgust, pressed the wet, painfully sobbing child to himself as tenderly as he could and ran with her through the garden, looking for another way out.
